newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Pacific Capital Assets float to proceed - NZ Herald.
newsitem.headline: Pacific Capital Assets float to proceed - NZ Herald.

text.p: Promoters of the Britomart-based Pacific Capital Assets will continue with float plans despite the project failing to obtain key planning consents, the New Zealand Herald reported on Tuesday.
The Herald quoted central promoter Jihong Lu as saying the decision would have no impact and that plans for the float would continue.
Promoters were visiting financial advisers in Kuala Lumpur on Monday when the Auckland Regional Council announced it had declined key consents needed for the Britomart project.

Responsibility for the resource consents falls on the Auckland City Council. Its harbour edge committee will meet on Thursday and is expected to recommend an appeal against the regional council ruling.
Mayor Les Mills said a year's delay for the project could mean prices in the fixed-price contract would have to be renegotiated.

But he and the other parties -- NatWest Markets Australia as developer, Walter Bau of Germany and subsidiary Concrete Constructions of Australia as contractors and Britomart Developments as assigned developer -- remained positive.

"I would expect we've got a good show of getting urgency (in the Environment Court) so we could get a spade in the ground by Christmas. If we don't get urgency it will push the project back 12 months," Mills told the Herald.
Peter Cross, who put the Britomart project together, said the developers would wait for the council's next move.
"It's the council's responsibility to deliver the resource consents. If they don't deliver the consents, I guess the contract collapses -- but they've got to do everything to obtain the consents."
While the appeal process was considered, Cross said the Britomart partners would continue with their planning and with the Pacific Capital Assets float.

The main impact on the float is likely to be a lower New Zealand retail investment level, and consequently larger Asian component in a listed company designed to build investment in Australian, New Zealand and South-east Asian infrastructure developments.
The project covers five hectares of downtown Auckland and is intended to give the city a new central transport terminal underground, in place of the rundown above-ground bus station.
It has been severely criticised by community interests concerned that the city council is creating a big liability.
Pacific Capital's prospectus has gone to the Stock Exchange and Companies Office for approval, but the sum being sought from investors has not been stated.

Doug Cholmondeley-Smith, chairman of the regional council's hearings commission, said the commission declined the consents because the city council had not established that de-watering would not result in damage to neighbouring buildings.
